facts.title: CodeGrep: An RL-Trained Retrieval Agent for LLM Coding Agents
facts.event_hint: CodeGrep: a 14B retrieval agent trained with GRPO to issue parallel grep/glob/read calls, injected into a frozen OpenHands agent on SWE-Bench Verified, preserving resolve rate while cutting rounds 15% and tokens 19%.
facts.problem: Modern LLM coding agents (Claude Code, OpenHands) spend most of their token budget finding the file to patch rather than patching it. On SWE-Bench Verified a 30B OpenHands agent averages 23 rounds and 631K tokens per resolved issue, dominated by grep, glob, and view_file calls in ambiguous exploration loops, often 20+ rounds in a wrong direction.
facts.mechanism: CodeGrep is a 14B-parameter retriever built on Qwen3-14B-Instruct, trained end-to-end with GRPO to emit up to 8 concurrent grep/glob/read tool calls per turn over a Git-worktree environment and return candidate files. Its output is injected into a frozen downstream coding agent (only the retriever is trained). A reward-design study compares three iterations; the final v3 moves the efficiency signal from the reward layer to the advantage layer and drops an auxiliary line-range term. Supervision is mined via CATM from 67K open-source agent trajectories.

evidence.claim: On all 500 SWE-Bench Verified instances, injecting CodeGrep lifts resolve rate from 25.8% to 27.0% (+1.2 pp) while cutting resolved rounds 23.0 to 19.6 (-15%) and resolved tokens 631K to 514K (-19%).
evidence.baseline: No-retrieval OpenHands baseline (25.8% resolve, 23.0 rounds, 631K tokens)
evidence.condition: SWE-Bench Verified, 500 instances, frozen OpenHands + Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507

evidence.claim: Downstream utility follows a precision threshold across three retrievers: BM25 at file-precision 0.375 hurts the agent, Jina at 0.445 is neutral, and only CodeGrep at 0.677 crosses the threshold at which retrieval begins to buy efficiency.
evidence.condition: Three injected retrievers on the same agent stack
evidence.source_locator: Abstract (PDF Page 1); Section 5.1 / Table 2, PDF Page 6

evidence.claim: BM25 injection degrades the agent: resolve drops 0.6 pp and resolved tokens inflate 21% (631K to 763K); on the 94 instances both configs resolve, BM25 rollouts spend 6.6% more rounds and 38.6% more tokens.
evidence.condition: BM25-injected OpenHands

evidence.claim: Reward design matters: applying the efficiency signal at the advantage layer (v2/v3) holds KL-to-reference at 0.09/0.15, versus reward-layer multiplicative scaling (v1) drifting to ~0.31 by step 900, i.e. roughly tripling policy drift.
evidence.condition: GRPO training, ~900-step run, 8xB200

evidence.claim: Training scale: 67,074 raw trajectories mined (CATM) yield 31,977 effective training samples (47.7% retention); end-to-end wall-clock is ~27 hours on a single 8xB200 node, early-stopped at step 897 of a planned 2000.
evidence.condition: ms-swift + LoRA + vLLM-colocated rollout

facts.evaluation_context: SWE-Bench Verified (500 instances); downstream agent is OpenHands with Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 (temperature 0, 100-round max). Retriever is CodeGrep 14B on Qwen3-14B-Instruct, emitting up to 8 parallel tools/turn, max 4 turns (3 exploration + 1 answer), 32 max tool executions per rollout. Training on a single 8xB200 node with LoRA via ms-swift. Retriever quality measured by file-level F-beta and precision (Table 2): CodeGrep v3 F-beta mean 0.576, precision 0.677, F-beta>=0.8 on 43.0%, 2.3 turns. The 25.8% baseline reproduces the published 25.2 +/- 0.7%.
facts.limitations: The resolve-rate lift is small (+1.2 pp). Only one downstream agent stack is evaluated (OpenHands); retriever effect on other agents (e.g. Cursor, Windsurf Cascade) may differ, and the dropped line-range term could benefit agents whose editor consumes line ranges. LoRA (not full fine-tune) is used, and the model is released as such. The reward-design conclusions are specific to this GRPO/CATM setting.
facts.project_relevance: Directly relevant to reducing code-agent read/grep/glob overhead. It shows a specialized 14B retrieval agent can shorten exploration while preserving task success, and it gives a practical decision rule (a file-precision threshold around 0.45-0.67) for when injecting a retriever starts to buy efficiency versus hurts the agent. The advantage-layer efficiency signal is a concrete RL-design lesson for tool-using agents.
source_notes: Resolve/rounds/tokens figures and the precision-threshold characterization are from Tables 2-3 and Section 5.1 (PDF Pages 5-6).
KL-drift comparison (0.09 vs 0.31) is reported in the Contributions (PDF Page 2) and Figure 2 (PDF Page 6).
Training scale numbers are from Section 3.6 and Table 5 (PDF Pages 5 and 12).

facts.title: Deep Agentic Search for Repository-Level Code Question Answering: An Empirical Study
facts.event_hint: Empirical study on SWE-QA comparing semantic (vector-index) search against deep agentic search (grep-by-subagent) for repository-level code QA, finding retrieval both more accurate and cheaper.
facts.problem: Code agents spend much of their effort locating code. The increasingly preferred design, deep agentic search, delegates exploration to an isolated subagent to protect the main agent from context pollution (context rot), but there has been little evidence on whether it actually produces better answers, and at what cost.
facts.mechanism: Two architectures are compared head-to-head on a shared benchmark: a ReAct agent using a prebuilt vector index over the repository (semantic search), and a Deep Agent in which a planning orchestrator delegates exploration to an isolated subagent that returns only a condensed result (deep agentic search). Every failed run is then coded into a six-mechanism, five-symptom failure taxonomy derived from execution traces.

evidence.claim: Pooled over four language models on SWE-QA, semantic search answered 65.2% of questions correctly versus 46.2% for deep agentic search.
evidence.condition: SWE-QA, pooled over 4 LLMs

evidence.claim: Semantic search produced each correct answer at less than half the cost of deep agentic search; Table 3 mean cost per pass for Gemini 2.5 Flash is $0.213 (semantic) vs $0.436 (deep agentic), and for Gemini 2.5 Pro $1.048 vs $1.526.
evidence.value: < half the cost per correct answer
evidence.condition: SWE-QA, 4 models

evidence.claim: The single largest share of deep agentic failures, 41.8%, occurred at the planner-to-subagent hand-off (coordination breakdown), a failure mode impossible for the flat semantic agent; the architecture-failure association is very strong (chi-square 508.8 on 5 d.f., Cramer's V 0.56).
evidence.condition: Coded failure set, 4 models

evidence.claim: The within-model Pass-rate advantage for semantic ranged from 5.6 percentage points (Gemini 2.5 Flash) to 49.6 (Gemini 3 Flash), with 10.0 (Gemini 2.5 Pro) and 10.6 (Qwen3-235B); all four McNemar and Wilcoxon tests remained significant after FDR correction.
evidence.condition: SWE-QA, per-model paired comparison

evidence.claim: Deep agentic hand-off failures were usually silent, ending in a fluent and confident answer that was wrong.
evidence.condition: Coordination-breakdown failures

facts.evaluation_context: SWE-QA benchmark (repository-level code QA); four LLMs: Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, Qwen3-235B. ReAct agent via LangChain (vector index, restricted to repo-structure lookup, retrieval tool, file reader) vs Deep Agent via LangChain Deep Agents framework (planning, virtual filesystem, sub-agent delegation). Fresh conversation thread per question; only the target repository available. LLM judge validated against an independent human panel on 800 stratified answers (human-vs-judge Cohen's kappa 0.74; human panel Fleiss' kappa 0.81).
facts.limitations: Scope is read-only repository-level code question answering (SWE-QA), not patch-writing/SWE-Bench-style tasks. The two architectures necessarily have different action spaces (tools differ), which the authors treat as intrinsic to the paradigms rather than a confound. Generalization is bounded by SWE-QA and the four models studied. Only the front evidence pack (abstract, intro, related work, design, master results Table 3, and failure taxonomy) was reviewed.
facts.project_relevance: Directly relevant to agent-acceleration (read/grep/glob). It quantifies that the widely adopted hierarchical grep-by-subagent design can be both less accurate and more costly than prebuilt vector-index retrieval for read-only repository QA, and it surfaces a concrete correctness risk: silent hand-off failures where the agent returns a confident but wrong answer. This challenges the assumption that context-pollution protection is free.
source_notes: Pooled accuracy figures (65.2% / 46.2%) match the average of the four per-model Pass rates in Table 3.
Cost-per-pass numbers and per-model breakdowns are taken from Table 3 (PDF Page 15).
Failure taxonomy statistics are from Section 6.3 (PDF Page 26).

facts.title: TensorCast: The Missing Tensor Management Layer in Large Language Model Infrastructure
facts.event_hint: TensorCast: a distributed tensor-management layer (Tensor-as-a-Service) that decouples tensor lifecycle management from computation, integrated with vLLM and SGLang; a programmable routing policy improves median TTFT by up to 93.2% under highly concurrent multi-turn agent workloads.
facts.problem: LLM infrastructure increasingly manages tensors (model weights, KV caches, checkpoints) as persistent distributed states, but existing systems optimize each task (weight loading, KV management, checkpoint sync) by deeply coupling task-specific mechanisms with execution engines, networks, or storage. This creates isolated silos that prevent reuse and cross-component composition, so operators repeatedly reimplement similar lifecycle logic and cannot express optimizations that span multiple components (e.g., jointly balancing load and preserving KV locality).
facts.mechanism: TensorCast proposes Tensor-as-a-Service (TaaS), decoupling tensor state management from computation. It provides first-class tensor abstractions, programmable lifecycle primitives (identify/place/materialize/transform/coordinate), and a runtime that separates tensor-management policies from execution mechanisms. Developers compose tensor-management programs via TensorCast APIs while transparently leveraging distributed execution and data movement; engine-specific state export/import is confined to an instance adaptor so callers evolve without modifying engines, transports, or storage.

evidence.claim: A programmable request-routing policy implemented with TensorCast improves median TTFT by up to 93.2% under highly concurrent multi-turn agent workloads.
evidence.condition: Highly concurrent multi-turn agent workloads

evidence.claim: For high-cardinality KV management (Qwen3-32B, TP=2) with RDMA enabled, TensorCast achieves TTFT reductions of 60% to 87.5% (2.5x to 8x speedup), comparable to the state-of-the-art Mooncake KV backend; with RDMA disabled it significantly outperforms Mooncake.
evidence.baseline: Mooncake KV storage backend in SGLang
evidence.condition: Qwen3-32B TP=2, LongBench prompts (~16k/35k tokens), 100% cache-hit stress test

evidence.claim: TensorCast accelerates model weight synchronization by 1.14x to 2.63x compared with the default updater, evaluated on Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B with the WeightPublisher helper publishing versioned weights that rollout workers retrieve per TP-rank slice.
evidence.baseline: Default SGLang updater (full weights from JFS)
evidence.condition: Two-node cluster, 4xH800 per node, RDMA disabled for fairness

evidence.claim: For the programmable router evaluation, three agentic workload presets are defined by inter-turn delay: fast (median 8.2 s), medium (median 20.1 s), slow (median 60.3 s); TensorCast's router shows the smallest cache-hit-rate drop as sessions scale, reducing request TTFT.
evidence.value: fast 8.2 s / medium 20.1 s / slow 60.3 s median inter-turn delay
evidence.condition: Agentic coding workloads, varying session number

evidence.claim: At Qwen3-235B-A22B (TP=8) TensorCast is again comparable to Mooncake under RDMA and better without; TP=8 introduces 4x more concurrent KV-page retrieval requests than TP=2, increasing contention and reducing TTFT improvements for both systems.
evidence.value: comparable (RDMA) / better (no RDMA) than Mooncake at TP=8
evidence.condition: Qwen3-235B-A22B TP=8

facts.evaluation_context: Integrated with vLLM and SGLang. KV-management cluster (Section 6.3): N nodes, each 64 CPU, 1 TB DRAM, 8xH800 GPUs, 200 Gbps RDMA; LongBench prompts grouped ~16k and ~35k tokens; KV reuse stress test forces N-1 instances to concurrently retrieve KV pages (100% cache hit). Weight-sync cluster (Section 6.2): two nodes, 64 CPU, 500 GB DRAM, 4xH800. Models: Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-235B-A22B. Baselines: Mooncake (SGLang HiCache KV backend), default JFS weight updater, and load-aware / cache-aware request routers.
facts.limitations: The authors do not claim a general abstraction is inherently faster than every specialized implementation; TensorCast confines engine coupling to an instance adaptor (integration cost remains). Training-framework integration (Megatron-LM, DeepSpeed) is left to future work. The 93.2% median-TTFT headline is stated as an upper bound under highly concurrent multi-turn agent workloads; the exact preset/session-count condition producing that peak is not pinpointable from the reviewed figures. Without RDMA, gains come from a userspace mTCP implementation whose benefit is network-dependent.
facts.project_relevance: Directly relevant to state-aware network / KV-cache scheduling. TensorCast's value-add over pure per-GPU memory scheduling is precisely cross-component composition: a programmable router that jointly balances instance load and KV-cache placement (migrating requests with their KV caches) preserves cache locality and cuts TTFT, and a unified tensor abstraction makes KV transfer, weight sync, and checkpoint resharding reusable rather than siloed. This is concrete evidence for network/coordination-side value beyond GPU-memory scheduling.
source_notes: The 93.2% headline is from the Abstract (PDF Page 1); the router comparison is in Section 6.4 with Figures 10-11 (PDF Page 14).
KV-management and weight-sync numbers are from Sections 6.2-6.3 (PDF Pages 12-13).
Workload delay presets are from Table 3 (PDF Page 13).

evidence_gaps.question: Which exact agent-workload preset (fast/medium/slow) and session count produces the up-to-93.2% median TTFT improvement, and what is the absolute TTFT for the TensorCast router versus each baseline at that point?

facts.title: Code Isn't Memory: A Structural Codebase Index Inside a Coding Agent
facts.event_hint: SuperAGI Research runs a leak-audited, model-controlled causal ablation (Claude Opus 4.7 fixed) showing that adding a structural codebase index to the SuperCoder harness lifts file-localization acc@5 from 44.3% to 84.5% and resolve from 41.9% to 50.4% with no per-cell cost penalty.
facts.problem: Coding-agent harnesses interleave LLMs with repository retrieval, but retrieval implementations vary widely and there has been no clean causal measurement of whether a structural codebase index (semantic + lexical + call-graph) actually changes resolve or cost, because most prior work confounds retrieval with prompt, tool surface, and control loop.
facts.mechanism: A three-arm controlled study on a fixed model (Claude Opus 4.7) across three seeds: SC-ON (SuperCoder harness with codebase_search + codebase_graph engine tools), SC-OFF (same harness, same prompts, with exactly those two tools removed), and OpenCode (independent ripgrep-based agentic-grep harness). The within-harness SC-ON vs SC-OFF toggle isolates the index causally; localization is scored under 'View B' which strips engine-result paths (a pointer, not an arrival) so SC-ON and OpenCode are credited comparably. Run inside a leak-audited per-task sandbox with a unified token-cost gateway.

evidence.claim: The within-harness ablation moves View B acc@5 from 44.3% to 84.5% (paired Wilcoxon p < 0.0001) and resolve from 41.9% to 50.4% (paired p = 0.003), while per-cell mean cost is statistically null (p = 0.73) and turns and tokens both fall significantly.
evidence.condition: SuperCoder harness, Claude Opus 4.7 fixed, 3 seeds, View B localization, paired Wilcoxon; pairwise denominator n=80 (SC-ON vs SC-OFF)
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 9 (Discussion): 'View B acc@5 moves from 44.3% to 84.5% (paired Wilcoxon p < 0.0001), and resolve moves from 41.9% to 50.4% (paired p = 0.003); per-cell mean cost is statistically null (p = 0.73) while turns and tokens both fall significantly.'

evidence.claim: Across seeds, the index lands at a lower $/solved than agentic grep; the ablation effects exceed the across-seed standard deviation (0.7-3.3 pp on resolve and acc@5) by 3 to 10x.
evidence.value: effects exceed seed noise by 3-10x; $/solved lower than agentic grep
evidence.condition: 3 seeds, SWE-PolyBench Verified + SWE-bench Pro; consistent with recently-reported coding-agent benchmark noise floors
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 9: 'Across-seed standard deviations are 0.7-3.3 pp on resolve and acc@5 ... the reported ablation effects exceed this noise by 3 to 10x.'

evidence.claim: The cross-harness check shows SC-ON does not regress against the OpenCode agentic-grep baseline on resolve (p = 0.087) or View B acc@5 (p = 0.080), directionally favoring SC-ON but not at conventional significance; the within-harness ablation is the cleaner read.
evidence.value: resolve p=0.087; acc@5 p=0.080 (marginal, directional SC-ON favor)
evidence.condition: Claude Opus 4.7 fixed, 3 seeds; pairwise denominator n=78 (SC-ON vs OpenCode)
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 9: 'The ON vs. OpenCode comparison on resolve and View B acc@5 is marginal at multi-seed (paired Wilcoxon p = 0.087 and p = 0.080 respectively); the within-harness ablation is the cleaner read.'

evidence.claim: The study runs on 91 instances across three languages (34 Go, 20 Java, 37 Python) from SWE-PolyBench Verified and SWE-bench Pro, with a 30-minute wall-clock cap (fired on two cells: one SC-OFF, one OpenCode; SC-ON's longest legit cell ran 19 minutes) and no turn or dollar cap.
evidence.value: 91 instances (34 Go, 20 Java, 37 Python); 30-min cap; SC-ON max legit cell 19 min
evidence.condition: pass@1 per seed, 3 seeds; statistics as mean of seed means with across-seed SD
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 4 (Section 4.4 Run scope): 'The study runs on 91 instances across three languages: 34 Go, 20 Java, 37 Python ... The 30-minute wall-clock cap fired on two cells in the released set (one SC-OFF and one OpenCode); SC-ON's longest legit cell ran 19 minutes.'

evidence.claim: The ablation isolates the index causally: SC-ON and SC-OFF differ only in the two engine tools (codebase_search, codebase_graph); model, prompts, sandbox, scorer, seeds, caps, and the remaining tool set are held identical, so the within-harness deltas read causally on the index.
evidence.value: causal ablation: only codebase_search + codebase_graph differ between SC-ON and SC-OFF
evidence.baseline: SC-OFF (identical except two engine tools removed)
evidence.condition: Leak-audited per-task sandbox; unified provider gateway for token cost; View B localization extractor applied uniformly
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 4 (Section 4.1 Arms) and PDF Page 9 (Discussion): 'The only thing that changes between SC-ON and SC-OFF is the engine toolset, which gives the ablation its causal reading ... model, prompts, sandbox, scorer, seeds, caps, and the remaining tool set are held identical, so the within-harness deltas read causally on the index.'

facts.evaluation_context: Benchmarks: SWE-PolyBench Verified (multi-language: Go, Java, Python) and SWE-bench Pro (longer-context Python); 91 instances total. Model: Claude Opus 4.7 (claude-opus-4-7) fixed across all arms and seeds. Arms: SC-ON, SC-OFF (within-harness ablation), OpenCode (cross-harness agentic-grep comparator). Three seeds, pass@1 per seed; paired-n denominators 80 (SC-ON vs SC-OFF), 78 (SC-ON vs OpenCode), 75 (triple intersection). Infrastructure: per-task isolated container, uniform image, unified provider gateway for token-level cost; 30-min wall-clock cap, no turn/dollar cap. Released artifacts: per-cell exclusion ledger, leak-audit script, dual-view localization extractor, full results DB.
facts.limitations: Single-model scope (only Claude Opus 4.7) — acknowledged as an intentional control trade. JavaScript and TypeScript are not covered (logged limitation). The cross-harness SC-ON vs OpenCode comparison is marginal at multi-seed (p=0.087 resolve, p=0.080 acc@5), so only the within-harness ablation is statistically clean. Closed-source harnesses (Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf) are out of scope by design. The sandbox backend configs/image spec are not public; per-cell patches, per-trace JSON, prompts, and sandbox image references are withheld (licensed source / internal config).
facts.project_relevance: Directly relevant to the agent-acceleration / context-building direction: it provides the first leak-audited, model-controlled causal evidence that a structural codebase index materially improves coding-agent file localization (+40 pp acc@5) and resolve (+8.5 pp) at no per-cell cost penalty and lower $/solved than agentic grep — i.e., structural ranking pays off precisely for multi-file change workloads, reducing repeated grep/read and context-rebuilding latency.
source_notes: Primary source: arXiv:2606.22417v1, Bhola et al. (SuperAGI Research), 21 Jun 2026; document.fetch_status=FETCHED.

Headline localization (44.3%->84.5%) and resolve (41.9%->50.4%) gains are stated with paired p-values, the exact ablation contract (only two tools differ), and the seed-noise context (0.7-3.3 pp) on PDF page 9.
